## My thinking for this year

I'm 67 now, been working these fields for 45 years. My wife and I are the only ones left at home — the kids are in town with jobs, they help out when they can but I can't count on them for the busy seasons. That reality shapes everything I decide.

I've got 16.1 mu split into two pieces. About 10 mu is my wheat-maize ground — the better soil, closer to the well. The other 6.1 mu I keep in cotton. I've thought about dropping cotton because the picking wears me out, but I know that crop and the price has been decent. I'll keep it one more year, but I'll have to hire labor for picking like I did last year.

**Wheat** — already in the ground since last October. I planted Jimai 22, same as the last few years, it holds up well here. I put down a compound base fertilizer at sowing, maybe 40 kg of 15-15-15 per mu. Now coming into spring, I'll topdress urea at jointing — about 15 kg/mu of urea, which gets me roughly another 7 kg N. So total N around 18 kg/mu. That's close to what the extension station recommends for our target yield of 500 kg/mu. I'll irrigate at jointing and again at grain-filling if we don't get rain. Pre-winter irrigation I already did in November.

**Maize** — right after wheat harvest in mid-June, very tight window, maybe 5 days. I use a hired custom planter with no-till direct seed, saves time and moisture. I plant Zhengdan 958 hybrid, proven variety. Base compound with the planter, then topdress urea at big flare stage. Total N around 15 kg/mu — maize responds well but I don't push it, the yield comes mostly from the variety and timing. One or two irrigations depending on the summer rain. Usually I get around 520 kg/mu.

**Cotton** — I plant mid-April under plastic mulch, that's non-negotiable here for getting the heat units. I keep using a Bt variety for bollworm resistance, still need some spraying for aphids and mites. Cotton needs less nitrogen than grain but more phosphorus and potassium — I use a cotton-specific compound at planting plus a topdress at flowering. The big expense is the picking labor — 6.1 mu takes me and my wife weeks, so I hire three women from the village for about 10 days total across the three pickings.

Budget's tight but manageable. Well water is metered so I only irrigate when I really need to. I keep some cash back for emergencies — at my age I don't take big risks anymore.
